text: BM25 is a bag-of-words ranking function that scores documents using term frequency, inverse document frequency and document length normalization.
Dense passage retrieval encodes questions and passages with two separate BERT encoders and ranks passages by the dot product of their vectors.
HyDE prompts a language model to write a hypothetical answer, embeds that synthetic document, and uses it to search the corpus without relevance labels.
Cross-encoders concatenate the query and the document into one input so that attention can model token interactions, producing more accurate relevance scores at higher cost.
HNSW builds a multi-layer proximity graph where upper layers are sparse, enabling greedy search with roughly logarithmic complexity.
Product quantization splits vectors into sub-vectors and replaces each with the index of its nearest centroid, compressing embeddings for memory-efficient search.
Reciprocal rank fusion combines several ranked lists by summing the reciprocal of each document's rank plus a constant.
Normalized discounted cumulative gain rewards relevant documents near the top of a ranking by dividing gains by the logarithm of their position.
Mean reciprocal rank averages the inverse rank of the first relevant result across a set of queries.
Query expansion with pseudo relevance feedback adds terms from the top retrieved documents to the original query before searching again.
ReAct interleaves reasoning traces with tool actions, letting a language model plan, call external tools and update its plan from observations.
Chain-of-thought prompting asks a model to produce intermediate reasoning steps, which improves accuracy on arithmetic and multi-step questions.
Self-consistency samples many reasoning paths at nonzero temperature and selects the answer that appears most often.
Toolformer teaches a language model to decide when to call APIs such as a calculator or search engine by self-supervised filtering of useful calls.
The Model Context Protocol standardizes how applications expose tools, resources and prompts to language model clients over JSON-RPC.
JSON-RPC 2.0 is a stateless remote procedure call protocol whose messages carry a method name, parameters and an identifier for matching responses.
Sentence-BERT fine-tunes BERT in a siamese network so that sentence embeddings can be compared with cosine similarity efficiently.
Contrastive learning with in-batch negatives trains an encoder by pulling paired examples together and pushing other examples in the batch apart.
Hard negative mining selects incorrect documents that the current retriever ranks highly, making training examples more informative.
Knowledge distillation trains a small student model to imitate the output distribution of a large teacher model.
Retrieval-augmented generation conditions a language model on passages fetched from an external corpus to ground its answers.
Hierarchical chunking indexes small child chunks for precise matching and returns their larger parent chunks to provide context.
Sentence window retrieval embeds single sentences and expands each hit with neighbouring sentences before generation.
Maximal marginal relevance reranks results by balancing similarity to the query against redundancy with already selected results.
Inverted indexes map each term to a postings list of documents that contain it, which makes keyword search fast.
Byte pair encoding builds a subword vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent pair of adjacent symbols.
The transformer architecture relies entirely on self-attention and feed-forward layers, removing recurrence from sequence modeling.
Positional encodings inject information about token order into transformer inputs because attention itself is permutation invariant.
Layer normalization rescales activations across the features of each example, stabilizing the training of deep networks.
Dropout randomly zeroes a fraction of activations during training to reduce overfitting.
Low-rank adaptation freezes pretrained weights and learns small low-rank update matrices, making fine-tuning cheap.
Instruction tuning fine-tunes a language model on many tasks phrased as natural language instructions to improve zero-shot generalization.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback trains a reward model on human preference comparisons and optimizes the policy against it.
Direct preference optimization fits a policy to preference pairs with a classification-style loss, avoiding an explicit reward model.
Self-rewarding language models act as their own judges, generating and scoring responses to create new preference data iteratively.
Beam search keeps the highest scoring partial sequences at each decoding step instead of only the single best token.
Nucleus sampling draws the next token from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold p.
Perplexity is the exponential of the average negative log-likelihood and measures how well a language model predicts text.
Multi-agent systems split a task among specialized agents, such as a planner, a coder and a critic, that coordinate through shared state.
A blackboard architecture lets independent components read from and write to a shared memory that a controller schedules.
Loop detection in agent systems hashes the relevant state each turn and stops when the same fingerprint repeats.
Episodic memory stores the trace of a single task, while semantic memory keeps distilled knowledge that persists across tasks.
Prompt injection hides adversarial instructions inside retrieved content or tool output to hijack a language model agent.
Sandboxing executes untrusted generated code in an isolated environment with limited filesystem, network and time.
Function calling lets a model emit structured arguments that match a JSON schema so applications can invoke tools reliably.
Cosine similarity, inner product and Euclidean distance give identical rankings when all vectors are normalized to unit length.
ColBERT keeps one embedding per token and scores documents with late interaction, summing maximum similarities between query and document tokens.
SPLADE learns sparse lexical representations with term expansion so that neural relevance can be served from an inverted index.
The BEIR benchmark evaluates zero-shot retrieval across heterogeneous datasets such as biomedical, financial and argument retrieval.
Caching embeddings of unchanged documents avoids recomputing them on every indexing run and reduces cost.
